messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: blocked split-plot ANOVA with fixed and random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been extremely remiss in posting a response to outline the final model that I have ended up with. I apologise, but better late than not at all, since I hope others find this thread useful.
After the helpful advice I received here, some reading, and discussion with a statistician here at Northern Arizona University, I came up with the following analytic approach:

I first have to define an explicit nesting structure, to be certain that lme4 can recognise the sample design. I then put the split-plot block design structure in the random effects, allowing for random intercepts. The random effect structure was not tested for significance (or explanatory power) because it is an integral part of the experimental design and therefore should not be excluded, even if the random effect offers no model improvement. In the summary output I can look at the variance associated with each random component, in order to understand where most of the variation lies.
In order to account for the repeated measures aspect of the experiment I include a categorical year effect in the random effects, and allow the intercept to be different in each year of the study. This allows the 'starting point' of each year to be different. The effect of change through time is tested by including a continuous time variable, centered on 0, in the fixed effects. This tests whether the slope through time is significant. Centering the variable is useful because it constrains the model to the time interval over which I have data; I do not want 2009-2013 as real numeric values, since that makes no sense. My starting year is 2009, not calendar year 0.
The other fixed effects are treatments, I set a reference for each treatment, to make sure that the model intercepts represent the 'control' treatment. By allowing full interactions: WW*SW*time I am able to represent the crossed nature of the WW*SW treatment and can test whether the changes through time differ with treatments.

Finally, I can look at the summary output of the model, calculate confidence intervals for the fixed effects (not-overlapping zero is significant at the 95% CI), and determine residuals of the fixed and random effects.

Code below:
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(lme4)
library(sjPlot)

# Prepare the data for stats
# data that contains the CO2 flux (NEE.sum) dependent response variables, and independent predictor variables: WW, SW, and WW x SW treatment, years that the experiment ran

data2 <- flux.variables

# make unique variables for each nested unit for clarity, lme4 will recognise the implicit nesting
data2$block <- as.factor(data2$block)

# make model with fence coded 1-2 and plot coded 1-4, then create unique names for each fence, WW or plot
data2$fence_2 <- ifelse(data2$fence == 1 | data2$fence == 3 | data2$fence == 5, "1", "2")
data2$plot_4 <- ifelse(data2$plot == 1 | data2$plot == 5, "1",
                       ifelse(data2$plot == 2 | data2$plot == 6, "2",
                              ifelse(data2$plot == 3 | data2$plot == 7, "3","4")))

data2$fence_2 <- as.factor(data2$fence_2)
data2$plot <- as.factor(data2$plot)
data2$plot_4 <- as.factor(data2$plot_4)

# create variable for random structure
data2 <- within (data2, {
  wholeplot <- factor(block:fence_2:WW)
  SWplot <- factor(block:fence_2:WW:SW) # this is in case I want to nest SW
  subplot4 <- factor(block:fence_2:WW:plot_4)
})

# stats lab consultation with Derek Sonderegger:
# For repeated measures
# make time a continuous variable to put in main effects (to test year effect)
# and make year a categorical variable and include in random effects

# center time on 0 so that 2009 is used as the reference year
baseyear <- min(data2$year)
data2$time <- as.numeric(data2$year - baseyear)

# make year a factor:
# categorical variable to put in random structure (time will be continuous as fixed effect),
# year effect will account for the offset from the overall trend throught time
data2$year <- as.factor(data2$year)

# reorder levels of time and treatment in the data to make sure that control in year 2009 is the reference
# for the intercept
print(levels(data2$treatment))
print(levels(factor(data2$time)))

data2$treatment <- relevel(data2$treatment, ref="Control")
print(levels(data2$treatment))

# The data look like this:
 year fence  treatment block SW WW    NEE.sum      fence_2  plot_4      subplot4  SWplot       wholeplot    time
1: 2009     1        Air        A      S  C        -29.318239       1            1            A:1:C:1     A:1:C:S     A:1:C          0
2: 2009     1    Control     A     C  C         3.934905         1             2           A:1:C:2     A:1:C:C     A:1:C          0
3: 2009     1        Air        A      S  C       34.577143         1            3         A:1:C:3        A:1:C:S     A:1:C          0
4: 2009     1    Control     A     C  C        3.516462         1             4        A:1:C:4          A:1:C:C     A:1:C          0
5: 2009     1 Air & Soil    A      S  W      -13.604757       1             1        A:1:W:1        A:1:W:S     A:1:W         0
6: 2009     1       Soil        A     C  W        -3.140330       1             2        A:1:W:2        A:1:W:C     A:1:W         0

# Model1:
# WW * SW * time: effects of treatment over time;
# WW is nested and SW is crossed (split-plot design);
# WW is part of the random nesting structure;
# whole plot is: block/fence/WW;
# subplot is block/fence/WW/plot

model1 <- lmer(NEE.sum ~ WW * SW * time + # use * or + depending on the interactions you want to specify
                 (1 | block/fence_2/wholeplot/subplot4) + (1|year),
               data = data2)

# display output of model and the effect size of each fixed effect
summary(model1)
# display the confidence interval around each fixed effect
confint(model1,method="boot",boot.type="norm",level=0.95,nsim=1000)

# I also want to know whether the distribution of residuals and model fit differ
# between the model with time and the model with environmental/biological predictors.
model1resids <- resid(model1)
model1fitted <- fitted(model1)
model1sqrtres <- sqrt(abs(resid(model1)))

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar = c(4,4,3,2))
plot(model1fitted, model1resids, main='resid, model1: WW*SW*time')
plot(model1fitted, model1sqrtres, main='sqrt resid, model1: WW*SW*time')
qqnorm(model1resids, main = 'model1: WW*SW*time')
qqline(model1resids)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))

# Look at the residuals and qqnorm plot from model1 of the random effects to see if they fall on the
# line (=normal).
# I believe that this will apply to all models with the same response variable since
# the RE structure remains the same.
# test the random effect quantiles - if they fall on the qq line, they are normal
sjp.glmer(model1, type="re.qq")

Marguerite
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hi folks,

I seek some help with a problem that does not seem to go away - the 1st input line in my file never appear in my output.

I am trying to perform Fisher's Exact paired tests on an input file with multiple rows (one row for each protein) and multiple columns (multiple biological properties), and adjusting p-value using FDR.

For each row (or protein), I want to compare whether each of its properties is statistically more abundant than expected by just chance.
The amino acid residue counts (for single protein, and sum total of all proteins) are therefore used for this calculation.

I am attaching an example input file, and my R code thus far (with various variation commented out).

I'd like the output to contain the protein ID as well as CoDomain classification information (as 'A' or 'P'), followed by adjusted p-values for each property (14 columns) for a row, iterated over each of the input rows.

When I convert table to dataframe, I am always missing input line #1 from the output. 654 input lines, 653 output lines!!!!

When I do NOT convert read.table to dataframe, I get only < 600 lines in output, compared to input file with 654 data lines.

I've tried several variations of my R script, but I am not sure about where I am going wrong - read.table? or cat / output step? elsewhere?
I hope someone can help fix the bug in my R script and explain to me what I was doing wrong, so I wont make this same mistake again.

Thanks!
Anand

Hi Anand,

I think your loop is okay, but the use of sink() might be the culprit. It looks like sink() works similarly to some of the graphics device functions, like pdf(). You open a path for your data to go, and then you close up that path after you’ve finished adding everything by bookending the sink() function call and the close() function call around the block of code that generates the output you want to save.

If I take out all of your uses of sink() and close() and just add a single call to sink(outfile) immediately before the loop, and a call to close(outfile) immediately after the loop, then it looks like the complete output file is generated.

I think the problem before was that the first sink(outfile) function call came as the *final* step of the loop. So the things in the loop worked great, the first row of output was printed to the screen, and THEN the file was opened for input. So the first time any results were actually written to that file was after the 2nd iteration of the loop.

I don’t know how common it is to use sink() and close() in your domain. I’ve never used them, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t the right choice for you case. Another way to do this without using sink() and close() would be:

1) Create a storage data frame just before the loop:

d <- as.data.frame(matrix(0, nrow=r, ncol=16))

2) Put the output from each iteration of the loop into the appropriate row (do this right after you make the ‘out’ variable):

d[i, ] <- out # Put the ‘out’ variable into the ith row of the d data frame

3) Check your work by looking at the the top 6 rows of d *outside* the loop.

head(d)

4) Write the variable to a csv file:

write.csv(d, outfile, row.names=FALSE)

--

We will explore examples of using regular expressions find transcription factor binding sites and to find regions of phage DNA (spacers) in bacterial genomes - key parts of the CRISPR bacterial immune system. We will also explore how to build a test suite for regular expression searches to ensure the regular expression pattern matching is accurate.

This workshop will be taught remotely and broadcast to UC Davis via Google Hangouts. It will also be streaming on YouTube.

In this half-day workshop, we will focus on using this library to find models that are good approximations of data. We will learn how fit different models to experimental data and how to compare different models to each other.

This workshop will be taught remotely and broadcast to UC Davis via Google Hangouts. It will also be streaming on YouTube.

For more information: http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/2016-02-19-scipy-lr.html

Hi Zach,

Welcome to the black-hole-vortex that is R! If I understand you correctly, these are your vairables:

1. inflamation marker
2. microbe genus
3. microbe abundance
4. time

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zach,

Welcome to D-RUG!

How to visualize really depends on what point you’re trying to illustrate with the data. You can map variables to at least x, y, color, and size of points and then facet over a fifth variable. Point shape is another possibility, but it’s not as visually obvious as the others. One naive idea that comes to mind for your data is a separate pairs plot for each time point in your dataset, something like this:
d = data.frame(
    marker1 = rnorm(300),
    marker2 = rnorm(300),
    marker3 = rnorm(300),
    time = rep(1:3, each = 100)
)
dsplit = split(d, d$time)
lapply(dsplit, function(df) pairs(df[, -4], main = paste('time', unique(df$time))))

You could also color points by time point instead of faceting over that variable. But again, the right approach will depend on what conclusions you want to illustrate, as well as the size of your dataset and other factors. One other thought is that if you are really interested in the correlations and not the values, it might make sense to extract the correlation between each pair of markers and visualize those, e.g. using the corrplot function from the package of the same name.

We’d love to see you at the meetings, but note that they are Tuesdays this quarter: 3 - 5 in Wickson 2124. Cheers,

Hi Zach,

There is quite a lot of missingness in this data. You can tell cor() how to handle missingness with the use argument (see the “details” section of ?cor), but even having it scrape out every comparison it can make, there are some variables in your dataset that don’t share any observations, so you cannot calculate a correlation between them. cor returns NA for those, and corrplot won’t deal with NAs… that’s what produces the error you saw. To make it work, you could remove the columns with the worst missingness and/or have cor calculate correlations based on just where two variables both have an entry:
sum(complete.cases(d))
(missingness = sapply(d, function(x) sum(is.na <http://is.na>(x))) / nrow(d))
d = d[, missingness < .5]
dcor = cor(d, use = 'pairwise.complete.obs')
library(corrplot)
corrplot(dcor)
​

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am graphing the results of an experiment where I tried a different aquatic invertebrate sampling equipment in different habitat types. I had more potential samplers in some habitat types than others. I'd like to make a grouped bar graph where each habitat type is grouped together. I can do this pretty easily with ggplot2, however the resulting graph makes each of the habitat types equal widths, and changes the widths of the bars. I'd like to make each of the bars equal widths and change the width of the groups according to how many bars they have in them. Can anyone help? I feel like this shouldn't be this hard.

This is the code I used for the above plot:

pi4 = ggplot(inverts3, aes(x=target, y= mdiet, fill = Sample.type))
 pi4 + geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymax= mdiet + sediet, ymin = mdiet - sediet), position = "dodge") +
  ylab("proportion of catch important to fish diets") + ylim(0,1)

I've attached the inverts3 data file if anyone would like to take a stab at it. I'd also be interested in doing the same thing using facets instead of a grouped bar, but I've been having the same problem with the widths of the bars.
--

messages.body_plain:
The trick for this is to facet along the grouping variable. In facet_grid() there’s an argument space="free_x" that will cause plots’ width to be proportional to their x scale. This way you can break up the plots by “target” and place these plots side by side horizontally:
pi4 = ggplot(inverts3, aes(x=Sample.type, y= mdiet, fill = Sample.type))  # <-- Note no 'target' here
pi4 + geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymax= mdiet + sediet, ymin = mdiet - sediet), position = "dodge") +
  facet_grid(.~target, scales = "free_x", space="free_x") +  # <-- where the magic happens
  ylab("proportion of catch important to fish diets") + ylim(0,1)
​

Workshop announcement: Jupyter Notebook

Who: Titus Brown
When: March 9th, 2016
Times: 9:15 am - 12:15 pm
Where: 1010 Valley Hall, UC Davis Campus

This half day workshop will introduce biologists to Project Jupyter (formerly IPython Notebook). We will assume some minimal experience with Python, but people new to IPython Notebook/Project Jupyter are welcome to attend!

Project Jupyter is a literate data analysis environment (similar to knitr and Shiny) that supports over 40 different programming languages, including R and Python both. It can be used to build reproducible analyses for publication, collaborate over distances on data analysis, and build interactive tutorials and homeworks around data analysis.

More at:
http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/2016-03-09-jupyter-notebook.html

Register at:
https://www.eventbrite.com/e/jupyter-notebook-half-day-workshop-tickets-21073325885

If you register for this workshop but cannot attend, please release
your spot on EventBrite or contact Jessica Mizzi (jessic...@gmail.com).
If you register but do not attend (which takes up a spot that could have
gone to someone on our waitlist!), you may not be able to register for
future workshops.
